children: With no off-patent versions currently in development for 90% of brand-name biologics losing market exclusivity over the next decade, the U.S. faces a significant “biosimilar void" that could mean $189B in lost healthcare savings, according to a new industry report.

Out of 118 biological products that face patent expiries between 2025 and 2034, only 10% are set to face biosimilar competition, the Association for Accessible Medicines, a lobby group representing generic drugmakers, said in a report last week.

Titled “2026 U.S. Generic & Biosimilar Medicines Savings Report," the review comes at a time when pharmacy benefit managers, drugmakers, and health insurers continue to blame each other for soaring drug prices in the U.S.

Biosimilars are cheaper copycat versions of a group of complex molecules known as biologics, which are designed to treat conditions such as cancer and account for a growing proportion of U.S. healthcare expenditure. They include blockbuster drugs such as AbbVie’s

“Biosimilars often enter a marketplace where success is determined not by clinical value or lower cost, but by opaque contracting practices, rebate-driven incentives, and formularies that favor higher-cost reference products,” AAM said in the report.

“These dynamics undermine competition, limit patient access to lower-cost treatment options, and weaken the business cases for future biosimilars investment,” the group added. According to AMM, generics and biosimilars generated $496B in savings last year, a $30B increase from 2024, primarily led by generics, which accounted for 95% of those savings.

Biosimilar development mainly targets biologics with large sales prospects and near-term patent expiries, AAM said, noting that the competition is particularly robust for drugs with annual pre-expiry biologic sales exceeding $1B.

AAM added that drugmakers abuse the system by handing massive rebates to PBMs for selecting higher-priced brand-name drugs. “The payment and reimbursement systems out there are built to favor higher-priced brand products,” The Wall Street Journal reported, quoting Alex Keeton, executive director of the AAM’s biosimilars unit.

The U.S. biosimilar industry is also facing patent disputes on a significant scale, with the number of patents asserted in courts being more than 10 times higher than in countries such as the U.K. and Canada.

The Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA), a lobby group representing drugmakers, faulted PBMs for the biosimilar void and defended the U.S. IP system, which provides them years of market exclusivity for life-saving medicines.

“If policymakers want lower costs and faster competition, they should focus on insurer-PBM conglomerates—not the IP system that has delivered more than 900 new medicines since 2000,” a PhRMA spokesperson said.

The Pharmaceutical Care Management Association, a trade group for pharmacy benefit managers, said that “abuse of the patent system far too often blocks biosimilars from the market" and added that PBMs are planning to ensure that biosimilars are the primary option for patients.

title: Looming biosimilar void risks $189B in lost U.S. healthcare savings: report
